prompt: Hall A's servers draw 4.8 MW of electricity. Roughly how much heat do they release into the hall?
options: Much less than 4.8 MW, because computation stores energy
About 4.8 MW
About 9.6 MW, because of fan friction
explain: Computation stores a negligible amount of energy, so the electrical power becomes heat at about the same rate.

prompt: Why does every explainer in this course ask for a prediction before you can use the sliders?
options: To grade you
Because committing to a prediction makes the result stick and exposes misconceptions
To slow you down
explain: Predicting first improves understanding compared with only watching, and a wrong prediction tells the app which misconception to drill.

prompt: A site draws 12.6 GWh in a year, of which 10.5 GWh reaches IT equipment. What is its PUE?
explain: 12.6 / 10.5 = 1.20. The 2.1 GWh of overhead is the target for cooling and power-chain improvements.

prompt: The site upgrades all server power supplies to a more efficient model. Total facility energy falls. What happens to PUE?
options: It improves substantially
It stays roughly flat or gets slightly worse
It can't be computed any more
explain: Power-supply losses sit inside the IT boundary. IT energy falls, and the cooling load falls a little with it, so the ratio barely moves and can even rise. A good reminder to track total energy, not only PUE.

prompt: Ideal (Carnot) cooling COP for chilled water at 16 °C and condenser water at 30 °C? (Use kelvin.)
explain: T_cold = 289.15 K and the lift is 14 K, so 289.15 / 14 ≈ 20.7. Real chillers reach a fraction of this, and the fraction is a useful efficiency diagnostic you'll fit from plant data later.

prompt: What is ASHRAE's recommended server inlet temperature range?
explain: 18–27 °C is the recommended envelope. Allowable classes go wider, but controllers in this course treat 27 °C as the line not to cross.

prompt: Hall A's UPS is described as N+1, where the load needs four modules. What does that mean?
options: Five modules are installed, so any one can fail without dropping the load
Four modules are installed, each oversized by 25%
Eight modules are installed in two independent paths
explain: N+1 means one spare beyond what the load needs. Two fully independent sets, each able to carry the whole load, is 2N.

prompt: Utility power fails. What carries the IT load for the 10–15 seconds before the generators take over?
options: Thermal storage in the chilled-water loop
The UPS batteries or flywheels
Nothing: servers ride through on their own capacitors
explain: Generators need seconds to start and synchronize. The UPS bridges that gap. Cooling has its own, separate ride-through problem, which is why chilled-water storage exists.

prompt: In a year a site evaporates 54 million litres of water in its cooling towers while its IT equipment uses 30 GWh. What is its WUE?
explain: WUE = site water ÷ IT energy = 54,000,000 L ÷ 30,000,000 kWh = 1.8 L/kWh.

prompt: A site with PUE 1.25 runs entirely on grid power with an emission factor of 0.4 kg CO₂e/kWh. What is its CUE?
explain: Every IT kWh drags 1.25 kWh from the grid, so CUE = 0.4 × 1.25 = 0.5 kg CO₂e per IT kWh.

prompt: Which site gets the most free-cooling hours from a waterside economizer with a 16 °C chilled-water supply?
options: A humid coastal site where the wet-bulb rarely drops below 22 °C
A dry, high plateau where the wet-bulb is below 10 °C on most nights
A hot desert site, measured at midday
explain: The economizer works when the towers can make water colder than the chilled-water setpoint, and tower water can only approach the wet-bulb. Cool, dry air gives the most hours.

prompt: You raise the chilled-water supply setpoint from 10 °C to 16 °C and leave the condenser water alone. What happens to the chiller's work per unit of heat removed?
options: It rises, because warmer water carries less heat
It falls, because the lift shrinks and COP rises
It stays the same, because COP depends only on the refrigerant
explain: COP grows as the lift between evaporator and condenser shrinks. Warmer chilled water means less lift, so less compressor work per kW of cooling.

prompt: A 40 kW rack is cooled by air that warms by 12 K as it crosses the servers. Air's volumetric heat capacity is about 1.2 kJ/(m³·K). What airflow does the rack need?
explain: At steady state the air must carry away all 40 kW: V̇ = P ÷ (ρc_p ΔT) = 40 ÷ (1.2 × 12) ≈ 2.78 m³/s. Halve the temperature rise and you need twice the airflow.

prompt: A CRAH fails and the cold aisle climbs to 29 °C for twenty minutes. In ASHRAE terms, where is it?
options: Still inside the recommended range
Outside recommended, but inside the class A1 allowable range (15–32 °C)
Outside every class, so servers shut down at 28 °C
explain: Recommended is 18–27 °C. Short excursions into the allowable range are tolerated, but they cost reliability margin and the controller should pull back fast.

prompt: Two ways to spend 20 minutes before a test: re-read your notes twice, or close them, write down everything you remember, then check. Which gives better recall a week later?
options: Re-reading, because it covers more material
Retrieval from memory, even though it feels harder
They come out about the same
explain: Retrieval practice beats restudy on delayed tests, and it feels less fluent while you do it. That gap between feeling and result is why the app schedules reviews for you.
